setting: A fictional lunchtime discussion between colleagues about a current workplace question.

presentation.situation: {{name}} wants your opinion on {{question}} {{name}} thinks {{view}}. Say what you think, give two reasons or examples, and respond fairly to the other view.
presentation.opening: Here's a question for you: {{question}} I think {{view}}. What's your opinion?

brief.you_are: You are discussing an opinion with a colleague.
brief.situation: {{name}} wants your opinion on {{question}} {{name}} thinks {{view}}. Say what you think, give two reasons or examples, and respond fairly to the other view.
brief.task: State your opinion clearly, support it with two reasons or examples, and acknowledge the other view.
brief.done_looks_like: {{name}} knows your opinion and your reasons, and feels you listened to their view.

participants.name: You
participants.relationship: You are discussing an opinion with a colleague.
goals: State your opinion clearly, support it with two reasons or examples, and acknowledge the other view.

participants.name: {{name}}
participants.relationship: A colleague who enjoys a friendly debate

card.want: A real discussion, and to test your reasoning.
card.speech: Clear everyday English. Natural, not formal.
tactics: Give one reason for your own view

pressure.gentle: Patient. Gives the other person time.
pressure.balanced: Pushes back once on anything vague.
pressure.challenging: Keeps pressing for specifics, fairly and without insults.

objectives.evidence: The learner states a clear opinion.
alternatives: I think it is better, in my opinion.

objectives.evidence: The learner supports their opinion with reasons or examples.
alternatives: One reason is cost. For example, travel is expensive.

objectives.evidence: The learner acknowledges the other view.
alternatives: I see your point, but I still think that...

beats.orient: I asked your opinion. Start with: I think, or: In my opinion.

opportunity: Can you give me an example?
beats.orient: Now give me two reasons or examples. Start with: One reason is.
fallback: Can you give me an example?

signals: \b(?:i see your point|i understand|however|on the other hand)\b
opportunity: But what about what I said?
Don't you think I have a point?
beats.orient: I have a different view. Show that you heard it. Start with: I see your point, but.
fallback: Don't you think I have a point?
But what about what I said?

closing_line: Fair enough. That's a good way to look at it.

o1.good: A clear position in the first sentence.
o1.micro_lesson: Say: I think, or: In my opinion.
o1.model: In my opinion, it depends on the job, but mostly I prefer it.

o2.good: Reasons and examples make an opinion worth listening to.
o2.micro_lesson: Say: One reason is, and: For example.
o2.model: One reason is cost. For example, my travel takes two hours.

o3.good: Showing you heard the other side, before you answer it.
o3.micro_lesson: Say: I see your point, but.
o3.model: I see your point about cost, but I still think it is worth it.

variants.name: Ali
variants.question: is working from home better than working in an office?
variants.reason: new staff learn faster in person

variants.name: Rachel
variants.question: should meetings have a strict time limit?
variants.view: every meeting should stop at thirty minutes
variants.reason: people get more focused with a limit
